lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Kolberg, a little Baltic town, sometime in the 1740s.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: A drum rolls across the market square.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: A wagon creaks in, piled high with lumpy brown things.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: People sniff them.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Someone tastes one.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Then they offer one to a dog.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The dog sniffs it — and walks away.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Everyone agrees.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: These things don't smell, don't taste, and not even the dogs will eat them.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Oh, and the wagon?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It was a gift from the King.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Today, that King lies in a plain stone tomb in Potsdam, Germany.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And people still leave potatoes on it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: They're thanking him for a clever trick.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So, why was Europe afraid of the potato?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And was it, really?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The usual story: scared farmers, tricked by a clever king and a clever pharmacist.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But the old records tell a different story.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And it has six parts.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: One is a law that nobody can find.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Another starts in a prison camp.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And one is a field with guards who go home every night.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Whenever a famous story shows up, we'll check it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Myth, disputed, or on the record.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Six reasons, six puzzle pieces.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Fit them all, and the answer appears.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The potato comes from the Andes, the high mountains of South America.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In the 1530s, Spanish soldiers found them stored in village homes.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: By the 1560s, potatoes were cargo.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In 1567, barrels of them sailed from the Canary Islands to Antwerp.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And the shipping record still exists.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In 1588, two of them reached Clusius, a famous plant expert in Vienna.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: A painting of the plant followed.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Look at the name: Taratoufli.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That's Italian for little truffles.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In England, John Gerard printed this picture in 1597.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: He called them Potatoes of Virginia.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Wrong part of the Americas, by the way.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Even the name was a mess: papa, batata, patata.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And newcomers often didn't know how to plant it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Back in Kolberg, one grandmother piled them all in a heap and covered it with a little soil.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Now, famous story number one: Europe thought potatoes were poison.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: They're cousins of deadly nightshade, a poisonous plant.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The family link is real, but Gerard called them wholesome food, roasted or boiled.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And historian Rebecca Earle finds that poison fears weren't what held Europe back.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Piece one clicks in: STRANGER.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: A new plant, with a borrowed name and no instructions.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But strange isn't scary.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So how did it taste?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Let's go back to that dog in Kolberg.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Did that scene really happen?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It comes from the memoir of Joachim Nettelbeck, a sailor from Kolberg.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: He saw it as a small boy and wrote it down as an old man.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And Kolberg wasn't alone.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In 1765, France's famous Encyclopedia wrote an entry on the potato.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: However you cook it, it said, the potato is bland and floury.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It can't be counted among pleasant foods.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Ouch.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That's a one-star review.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But read on.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In five French regions, it says, potatoes were the everyday food of farm families.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: For much of the year!

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The experts were bored.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Farm families were already eating.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Part of the problem was status.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Potatoes had a name as filler food for the poor.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So far, nobody sounds afraid.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Bored, yes. Afraid, no.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Piece two: TASTE.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Not scary, just bland and a bit low-class.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So why are potatoes so hard to find in old records?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The answer is out in the fields.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Imagine you're a farmer in a German village around 1700.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Your village farms three huge fields.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Each year, one grows winter grain, one grows spring grain, and one rests.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That resting field is called fallow.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It gets a year off for the soil, and the cows graze there.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And the whole village follows one shared plan.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In one region of northern Germany, about 40 percent of farmland was resting.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So where do potatoes go?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Into the little garden behind the house.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And here's the clever part.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Farmers owed the church a tithe, one tenth of their harvest.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But a few rows by the kitchen door were easy to hide and hard to tax.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The tax man barely saw them.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Then potatoes crept into the resting fields.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And in 1802, church officials in Anhalt opened a whole file about it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Its title: the potato tithe from the fallow field.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Who gets a tenth of a potato?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Historians still argue about the timing.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Earle says farmers grew potatoes in many parts of Europe by the late 1600s.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Others say big potato fields only spread after 1800.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Both can be true: gardens early, fields late.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Piece three: FIELDS.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: No room in the plan, so it hid in the garden.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: We're past halfway, and the two most famous stories are still ahead.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: If you like stories checked against the record, subscribe.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But was the potato actually safe to eat?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Paris, 1771.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: France's finance minister sends a question to the city's top doctors.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Some provinces blame potatoes for making people sick.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Is that true?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The doctors' answer: potatoes are safe.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So the critics change their story.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Now potatoes harm the grain and wear out the soil.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Then there's a story all over the internet.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: France banned potatoes in 1748, over a rumor about leprosy.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Historians have looked for that law.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Nobody has found it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Earle traces that rumor to one secondhand note in a plant book from 1620.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Piece four: DOCTORS.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Real doubts, an official question, and no ban.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Remember the King who sent that wagon to Kolberg?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: He was just getting started.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Prussia, April 1746.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The first royal potato order goes out, in Pomerania, the region around Kolberg.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It aims to ease a shortage of bread.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Townspeople and farmers should work hard at growing garden crops, especially potatoes.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Ten years later, in 1756, came the most famous one.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Officials must explain why potatoes are useful, and urge people to plant them that spring.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: How many potato orders did Prussia send out?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: One, five, or fifteen?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Have a guess.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Fifteen.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Historians count at least fifteen potato orders.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: If you need fifteen orders, the first fourteen didn't quite work.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Now, Germany's favorite potato story.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Frederick plants a royal potato field and puts soldiers around it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Farmers think: if the King guards it, it must be valuable.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So at night, they sneak in and take some home.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Trick complete.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Potatoes everywhere.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Jürgen Luh, a historian for Prussia's old palaces, says there's no good evidence for it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: He adds that Frederick never ate a potato himself.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Not boiled, not fried.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The hero picture comes partly from paintings like this one.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It shows Frederick checking a potato harvest.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The artist painted it a hundred years after the King died.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So did farmers fight the potato?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Luh says many simply ignored the orders.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Many farmers weren't against potatoes.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: They already grew them in gardens, just not in big fields.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Piece five: ORDERS.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The state wanted potato fields long before most farmers did.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But orders alone didn't win the argument.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Hungry years did more.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And it starts with a prisoner.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In the 1750s and 1760s, France and Prussia are at war.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The Prussians capture a young French army pharmacist.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: His name is Antoine Parmentier.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: As a prisoner, he's fed potato mash, day after day.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Later, he'll spend decades promoting it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Then come the hungry years.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In 1770 and 1771, heavy rain ruins the harvests in the Czech lands.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Bread gets expensive.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Families go hungry.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In France, an academy in Besançon runs a contest.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Which plants could stand in for bread when harvests fail?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Parmentier answers with the potato, and wins.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Now, the French version of the trick.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Parmentier plants potatoes on a sandy army field outside Paris.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Guards watch it by day, and go home at night.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Curious Parisians sneak in and take the potatoes.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Sound familiar?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It's the same story as Frederick's field.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And it has the same problem.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: A colleague named Virey told it after Parmentier died.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Historians think Virey borrowed an older tale.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The field itself was real, though.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And in the 1780s, the story goes, he brings potato flowers to Versailles.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The King pins one to his coat.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Sources don't even agree on the year.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Hungry years made rulers take the potato seriously.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Officials and scholars started to see a well-fed people as a strong country.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Piece six: HUNGER.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And there's the full picture.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So, why was Europe afraid of the potato?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Mostly, it wasn't.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Europe wasn't so much afraid of the potato as unimpressed by it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And many of the scary stories were written later.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Remember that dog in Kolberg?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: He wasn't scared. Just unimpressed.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: For a long time, neither was Europe.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But once Europe gave it a real chance, it paid off.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: One last guess.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: From 1700 to 1900, how much population growth in Europe, Asia and Africa came from potatoes?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: About five percent, up to a quarter, or over half?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: About a quarter, say economists Nathan Nunn and Nancy Qian.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: A later review puts it between a sixth and a quarter.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And that tomb in Potsdam?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: People still leave potatoes on it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: They're thanking Frederick for a trick he probably never pulled.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Meanwhile, his fifteen real orders hardly get a thank-you.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Next time: how did humans invent glass?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Subscribe, and it'll show up for you.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Tell me in the comments: what food did you hate at first, and love now?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: See you next time.
